quizzes.question: If a medical test has 99% sensitivity and comes back positive, why can the actual probability of having the disease still be very low?

student_answers.answer: Because if the disease is very rare in the population, false positives among healthy people outnumber true positives.
It cannot be low—if the test is 99% accurate, you have a 99% chance of having the disease.
It depends on the prior probability P(Disease): with a 0.1% prevalence, most positive results are false alarms.
Because P(Positive | Disease) is different from P(Disease | Positive); we need Bayes' theorem to invert the conditional probability.
Because the test fails 99% of the time when patients are healthy.
I'm not sure, I think it's because the two events are always statistically independent.
Because we are ignoring the denominator P(Positive), the total probability of testing positive across both sick and healthy people.
If the test is 99% sensitive, the margin of error is only 1%, so you are almost certainly sick.

quizzes.question: What is the practical difference between independent events and conditionally independent events?

student_answers.answer: Two events can be dependent overall, but become independent once we condition on a third common-cause variable.
They mean the exact same thing; we just call it conditional independence when using Bayes' rule.
Conditionally independent means that P(A and B) = 0.
For example, fever and cough are correlated, but once you know the patient has the flu, knowing they have a fever gives no extra info about the cough.
It means A does not affect B only when we have no prior information at all.
